hansard.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
hansard.text: That is exactly the example I was coming to, because I imagine that Lords amendment 33 was designed some time over the summer to address the Hugging Face incident. The hon. Gentleman says “we are building” such systems. Well, for a start, I am not building them; they are being built by companies—hugely valuable businesses, as we saw with Anthropic's valuation. If they cannot control—or rather, I would say, design—tools and technologies that can be used by those who purchase them to achieve the ends or tasks they are supposed to achieve, then that is bad design. I think the hon. Gentleman's position is that this technology is so amazing that it is beyond human control or understanding, but that should certainly not be the case yet, and we have the AI Security Institute to test and to confirm that such technology is secure. His intervention goes to the heart of the issue: if this AI technology is beyond control or comprehension, what is it doing being sold in our markets? The Hugging Face incident was described as a loss of control, rather than as badly designed software or applications; that was partly anthropomorphisation of AI, but it also increased interest. The Science and Technology Committee has identified hype as one of the four key barriers to the effective digital transformation of the public sector, and I think that is what this incident was. Lords amendment 33 gives the Secretary of State powers over those who are seen to have lost “oversight or control of an AI agent”, but I would argue that it is actually those who have made, designed or developed the AI agent who have the power or ability to set the guardrails for achieving the tasks it is meant to achieve. I am concerned that this is, in effect, giving the Secretary of State power over those who do not act

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Victoria Collins
hansard.text: When the Liberal Democrats talk about a digital sovereignty strategy, it is about being realistic about this and looking at where we can build and get ahead. There is also an important element of leadership here—how can the UK develop those capabilities if we do not even start? DeepMind was started in the UK, yet in the past two years, people have told me time and again that we cannot build those models here. If we have given up, then of course we cannot. We also have to back British tech and businesses. When it comes to AI models—I will touch on other elements, too—we do not need frontier models for every single application; some need something smaller and more predictable. Whether it is building, partnering or shaping, we need to take this seriously, and sooner rather than later. In June, I asked the House to back our digital sovereignty strategy so that our critical infrastructure does not depend on a handful of foreign suppliers. Unfortunately, the Government turned that down, but we will keep making the case. In the light of the Microsoft outage, I ask the Minister what assessment has been made of the reliance of the Government and public services on foreign suppliers, because that is vital to our cyber-security and resilience. Turning back to the amendments before us, I thank colleagues in the Lords who have worked hard on improving the Bill. Lords amendment 107, which was passed with the support of Liberal Democrat colleagues in the other place, would require a comprehensive review of the NIS regime within 12 months of Royal Assent, building directly on what Liberal Democrats have argued from day one. On Second Reading, I warned that “the Bill leaves the back door wide open by leaving out key sectors”. —[ Official Report , 6 January 2026; Vol. 778, c. 190.] In Co

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Chris Vince (Harlow) (Lab/Co-op)
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to speak in this debate. I promise I will not go on too long. [Hon. Members: “More!”] Cross-party support already! I draw the House's attention to the fact that my father-in-law, Professor Robin Bloomfield, is a professor of system and software dependability at City and St George's University—I finally got his title correct. Also, the Kao data centre is in my constituency of Harlow. I thank the Minister for his opening statement, and particularly for his commitment to looking at increasing the scope of the Bill. We had conversations across parties in Committee on the scope of the Bill, and whether it could be extended to other potentially vital infrastructure. We live in uncertain times, and bad state actors, used by foreign powers, will seek to undermine our national infrastructure and our democracy using the internet and AI. We need to be alive to that. I rise to speak against Lords amendment 107. Although I am sure that it is well-meaning, I am concerned that it could have unintended consequences. It would require the Secretary of State to conduct an annual review of the effectiveness of the national infrastructure and security systems regime, and to lay that review in front of Parliament once it was complete. As you will know, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am always a huge supporter of parliamentary scrutiny, not least because it allows me to give a matter scrutiny. However, it is very likely that the foreign powers that we have concerns about are observing said debates and said scrutiny, so if the report highlights any potential weaknesses in the network and information systems, those powers will be aware of those weaknesses, which could put us at risk when they seek to exploit those weaknesses. Finally, Madam Deputy Speaker—I promised I would be short—I

hansard.speaker: Lord Young of Acton (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I declare my interest as director of the Free Speech Union and editor-in-chief of the Daily Sceptic . Amendment 101 in my name asks a simple question: do the Government hold a consistent view about how much proof of identity a citizen should have to show, and to whom? Clause 48, as we have been told, lets voters use a UK-issued bank card at the polling station. No photograph is needed, as my noble friends have pointed out. The only requirement is that the name matches the name on the electoral register. The Government's reasoning is that this will cut the proportion of electors without acceptable ID to less than 1%, notwithstanding the reservations just expressed by the noble Baroness. That is a laudable aim. Meanwhile, Section 214(a) of the Online Safety Act gives the DCMS Secretary of State the power to bring forward regulations requiring online service providers “to prevent or restrict access by children”. One option under consideration—the favoured option, as I understand it—is that users should have to prove their age with government-issued ID, namely a passport or a driving licence. A 16 year-old newly enfranchised by this Bill could therefore prove they are eligible to vote by producing a debit card in the morning, and then, in the evening, be asked to produce a passport or a driving licence to follow the election results online. That cannot be right. The Minister may reply that a voter's identity has already been rigorously checked before they are entered on the electoral register and that all the debit card does is confirm that they are the person named on the register. hansard.speaker: Brian Leishman (Alloa and Grangemouth) (Lab)
hansard.text: Although COP ended without agreement, Nvidia has seen its stock increase by 30%, taking the company to a nearly $4 trillion market capitalisation. Meanwhile, my constituents in Larbert continue the campaign to prevent a hyperscale AI data centre from being built in a residential area, which is next to a care home and a hospital that serves over 300,000 people. What is the Secretary of State doing to stop international investors and tech oligarchs with no regard for our climate trying to shape Britain's industrial future for their own gain, at the expense of communities?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Mark Pritchard
hansard.text: I have broken my own embargo, but there we are. On sovereign capability, the hon. Lady will know that the European Union is looking to build its own cloud capability, which I think makes sense, given the ups and downs of the transatlantic relationship over the past few months and the political views of some of those who are in charge of the big tech companies. Does she think that is something the UK should do independently, so that we have our own sovereign cloud capability, or at least something we should work on closely with partners and allies across the world, not just in the United States?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Ian Murray
hansard.text: Governments of all colours have recognised that the UK has to have a debate about tech and AI sovereignty. In parts of the tech stack, we should have greater AI sovereignty, because we are good at that stuff in this country, and in other parts, it would be impossible for us to try to compete. I accept the point and the challenge that if we are not in control of the levers, and they are controlled by other jurisdictions, it becomes much more difficult to determine how to regulate. We have to promote AI sovereignty for the technologies in the tech stack that we are good at. We have put in place the AI sovereign wealth fund, and we are ensuring that the national cloud infrastructure project is a partnership with the sector. There are not many suppliers, but we want to make sure that we use big Government procurement to ensure sovereignty in the cloud, and that we are seeding fledgling companies here. This is a process, but through our commitment to procuring quantum, and our £2 billion investment in quantum, the Government are showing industry very clearly that we are challenging for AI sovereignty in the tech stack in areas that we are good at. However, there are parts of the tech stack in which we will not be able to challenge.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Sir John Hayes (South Holland and The Deepings) (Con)
hansard.text: The Minister is showing responsiveness and flexibility, and I think he understands that, although the Bill does enjoy cross-party support, there is a need to get it right. Part of that is recognising that this is a highly dynamic environment and that technology moves very fast. What is probably in the their lordships' minds is that that requires a very regular reappraisal of the appropriateness of the application of policy. To that end—I raised this point last week when we debated artificial intelligence—I wonder whether the Minister might look at the whole issue of interoperability and interconnectivity. My fear is that we are concentrating risk, and when we review these matters we might want to consider that in a cross-departmental way.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
hansard.text: The hon. Lady anticipates the end of my contribution, which makes me think that maybe I should get to it faster—but yes, we need a comprehensive AI regulatory package that includes safety by design principles. That has been discussed by members of my Committee. On Cyber Essentials, will the Minister respond to this particular statistic? In 2024-25, 55,000 Cyber Essentials certificates were issued. There are about 6 million SMEs in this country, so at that rate it will take about 100 years before all small businesses are brought up to the cyber standard. Is it not essential that before we put such responsibilities on businesses deploying AI, or as we do so, we ensure that they have the tools and skills to do so in a well-informed and effective way? Right now, there is no testing for AI services. There are no guarantees that AI is safe. I would argue that any frontier model AI products and services sold in this country should, for example, have been through the Artificial Intelligence Security Institute's testing process. That is not the case at the moment. The Competition and Markets Authority indicated in a statement today that normal consumer protections apply to AI services. I am not sure where that leaves businesses. My key question to the Minister is: why is he putting the responsibility for AI behaviours on the buyers of AI, and not, it would seem, on the sellers? I was contacted by a major cyber-security company making exactly that point. What does “control” mean in this case? What if there was never any control, because AI models are non-deterministic and the concept of control may not be appropriate? What about the concept of safety by good design? Are we not taking a rather whack-a-mole approach? Would it not reassure business and ensure a more comprehensive ap

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Victoria Collins
hansard.text: The hon. Member, as always when there are synergies across the House, has predicted what I am about to talk about. I do agree. We welcome the amendments to take on the AI threats, but we need to look at future-proofing the legislation. If it is not AISI that will take that on, we need to have a single AI regulator that helps to keep us secure in the face of increasing cyber-security threats from AI. The Liberal Democrats support Lords amendment 107. We have pushed for it at every stage of the Bill, and the other place has agreed. Our asks of the Government are simple: to review every critical national infrastructure sector within a year; to review political parties, electoral infrastructure and advanced manufacturing; to make boards accountable; to ensure that the AI security regulations have the clarity and teeth they need, and a regulator; to take a holistic approach to our digital resilience; and to look at our sovereign capabilities. Our constituents and every business in our supply chains deserve nothing less.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Ian Murray
hansard.text: My hon. Friend is right about diversification, vendor lock-in, and there not being a wide array of choice in the marketplace for various aspects of technological embeddedness, in supply chains or otherwise. I absolutely get that challenge. There is a balance to be struck between flexibility and certainty in the regulations. I am very happy to look at the examples that my hon. Friend has given, but he is correct that in such a fast-moving technological landscape, we have to make sure that we cover as many bases as possible. The reason for this Bill is to update the 2018 regulations to bring managed service providers into scope, alongside others, and the review that I have announced tonight will look at whether that scope should be widened further, if things transpire in other parts of the economy. This year, AI incidents have shown that we face a new challenge in cyber-security. It is vital that our essential services remain well protected against novel risks. We have brought forward changes that will help us better understand why incidents involving AI occur, and help us share lessons across regulators and regulated entities. Lords amendments 33 to 40 and supporting amendments update the delegated powers in the Bill, clarifying that through future regulations the Government will be able to use in-house expertise such as the AI Security Institute to collect vital information about the causes and impacts of AI loss of control incidents occurring in essential services. I thank Members, particularly the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith), who is not in his place, for campaigning on the topic of information sharing. Lords amendments 21 to 24 restrict overseas information sharing by NIS regulators to our Five Eyes partners, European eco

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Victoria Collins
hansard.text: For our constituents, cyber-security is not an abstract debate. It is about whether their company can pay their salary, whether the food supply chain is stable and food makes it to their table, whether the council can keep its services running, and whether the personal details that they hand over when registering to vote stay safe. Last year's attack on Jaguar Land Rover was the most economically damaging cyber-event in UK history, costing an estimated £1.9 billion and hitting more than 5,000 organisations. Earlier this month, hackers took remote control of supermarket fridges and freezers in at least six European countries and warmed them until tonnes of food had to be thrown away. Researchers have found that more than 800 refrigeration and building control systems linked to British retailers can be reached over the open internet. This impacts the weekly shop for every family in our constituencies. The Bill was our opportunity to get ahead of those threats, to strengthen the systems that we all rely on and to secure our digital sovereignty. When it comes to building that sovereign capability, the IPPR offers a really solid framework: building where we can get ahead; shaping regulation and procurement; and partnering with other middle countries, such as the EU. The Minister talked about the AI sovereign fund. I will gently push on that, because I have talked to companies that are looking for investment from the fund and it seems that the definition of sovereignty is not actually that clear. We are not necessarily even talking about AI sovereign models, so I want to push for clarity on what the AI sovereign fund is funding. We need to think about this in terms of a whole digital sovereign strategy.

hansard.speaker: Lord Spellar (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, is there not a basic difficulty here in that, while it may be of great use to the security services to know who is talking to each other, if there is a back door to the actual content of the messaging, surely, in the age of AI, it will be found quite quickly?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Dr Ben Spencer (Runnymede and Weybridge) (Con)
hansard.text: I begin by thanking the Minister here and the Minister in the other place for their collaborative approach to these stages of the Bill. The UK faces a rapidly evolving threat landscape, to which we must be able to react and respond to ensure security. Those who seek to undermine our security and our critical national infrastructure are constantly adapting the tools and technologies they use, and our legislation must be capable of adapting with them. We must be clear about the threats we face, and in order to remain relevant, the legislation must address the actual risks, not just the tools that may be used. I put on record my thanks to colleagues in the Lords for their careful work in scrutinising and strengthening the Bill. The amendments before us raise important questions about how we measure the effectiveness of our cyber-security regime, how we counter threats from hostile states and how we ensure that our legislation keeps pace with emerging technology. Keeping our critical national infrastructure secure is essential in the modern world, so I hope that Ministers will consider the substance of these amendments carefully and make improvements where possible, while putting the security and resilience of the UK first. I will specifically address Lords amendments 107 and 108 and our amendments to Lords amendment 33, concerning autonomous systems. Amendment 107 would require the Secretary of State to review within 12 months the effectiveness of the Act and the network and information systems regulations, including on sectors within scope, the regulatory framework under which NIS regulations operate, and the obligations that could be placed on organisations and technology providers to improve their cyber-resilience. At its heart, the amendment raises an entirely legitima

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alison Griffiths
hansard.text: I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members' Financial Interests. After a recent career in cyber-security before coming to this place, I was proud to work with the shadow Minister in Committee. Lords amendments 107 and 108 build on that work, while amendments (a) to (i) to Lords amendment 33 seek to broaden its scope and effectiveness. Together, they are fundamental to ensuring the resilience of our critical national infrastructure. Lords amendment 107 seeks to ensure that our regulatory regime remains fit for purpose. I suggest that the effectiveness of the regime will depend on the quality and frequency of regulatory scrutiny. It is not just about enforcement, but about nuance. Compliance does not necessarily mean that an organisation has fully understood its cyber-risk. Does it have a cyber-security plan that makes clear that it understands and will mitigate inherent weaknesses in legacy infrastructure? Are regulators consistently demanding returns from operators of essential services and following up on shortcomings? Will the Minister address how that will be achieved consistently across regulators? On Lords amendment 108, I consistently raised in Committee the risks associated with intelligent electronic devices from individual manufacturers being deployed across multiple sectors of our critical national infrastructure, from water, electricity and rail to oil and gas. The register of foreign powers that pose a cyber-threat is useful, but it would be strengthened by understanding how IEDs and essential services could be deployed against us by those nations. The devices may be manufactured in such countries, or they could be manufactured elsewhere and then compromised by hostile actors, and they are spread right across the sectors that could compromise us

hansard.speaker: Viscount Camrose (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, what assessment have the Government made of the cyber security impact on British citizens and businesses of the withdrawal of Apple's advanced data protection service?

hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, the tribunal found that the Government's own briefings to the Times and the Financial Times , authorised at a senior level, undermined the secrecy they were asking the court to protect. Will the Government now commit to publishing the number of technical capability notices in force, and to giving the Investigatory Powers Commissioner a duty to report publicly on how they affect encryption, so that Parliament does not have to rely on litigation by Apple, Privacy International and Liberty to learn how these powers are used?

hansard.debate: VAT Exemptions: Retailers and Online Marketplaces
hansard.speaker: Lord Wilson of Sedgefield (Lab)
hansard.text: In 2001, the Government removed VAT relief for imports of up to £15 and made online marketplaces liable for VAT on goods sold by overseas businesses. This was highly successful and raised £8 billion, and it continues to raise about £1.8 billion a year. Customs de minimis relief on parcels up to the value of £135 will be removed by 2028 at the latest, raising a further £500 million per annum. Non-UK sellers will also be required to appoint a UK-based fiscal representative, who would assume joint and several liability for customs debts. The Government's approach has been welcomed by online platforms such as Amazon and eBay and will continue to be monitored after implementation. As I said, the proposals will raise an additional £1 billion for the high street. Of course the Minister will accept a meeting with the noble Lord.

hansard.speaker: Sir Ashley Fox (Bridgwater) (Con)
hansard.text: I thank the Secretary of State for advance sight of her statement. This Government told the British public that if we led the world on climate policy, the world would follow. Ministers have lectured industry, imposed extra burdens on households and sidelined concerns about competitiveness, all on the basis that Britain would provide the model that others would emulate, but even with 100 private jets touching down at Antalya, a British delegation of 255, and 92,000 people at the largest conference ever, the whole thing collapsed. After months of speeches, declarations and moral grandstanding, the outcome was failure. The truth is uncomfortable: while Britain has been busy making itself poorer in pursuit of climate leadership, the world's major powers have been moving in a very different direction. The United States did not even send a delegation to the conference. Instead, it is pursuing what it openly calls “energy dominance” to win the race for artificial intelligence and future technologies. Does that not expose the central flaw in the Secretary of State's approach? The rest of the world is focused on energy security and growth; meanwhile, this Government remain trapped in an ideological cage that assumes all nations share Britain's priorities. It is obvious that they do not. Perhaps the most revealing moment of COP31 was when the proposed text omitted any reference whatsoever to fossil fuels. That is because everyone can see that the world has become more dangerous and our energy security is at risk. This so perfectly demonstrates why the Government's approach is misguided. The Secretary of State believes that if Britain loses enough jobs, sacrifices enough investment and abandons enough industrial capacity, others will surely follow. I wonder what the GMB general se

hansard.speaker: Lisa Smart (Hazel Grove) (LD)
hansard.text: Civil servants have given years, often decades, of service to this country. They planned their retirement carefully, and they deserve to know that the pension that they earned will arrive on time. However, almost a year after Capita took over the civil service pension scheme, far too many of them still cannot be sure of that. The problems remain. In just the past couple of weeks, yet another constituent, Karen from Offerton, contacted me because she has been waiting for more than two months for her pension, despite providing six months' notice before retiring. Karen currently has no income. She has repeatedly been in contact with Capita, as her initial quote was incorrect, but Capita has failed to say when it will fix it. That is yet another example of Capita's failure. We have discussed these issues many times. Does the Minister feel that she has the tools she needs, through the Procurement Act 2023 or other legislation, to hold Capita properly to account and to get this situation sorted, or is she seeking additional powers?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: As I have set out in previous answers, the Procurement Act 2023 allows Government to take into account previous performance. I have met Capita executives on multiple occasions since I became the Minister for this portfolio, and I made clear in no uncertain terms that their performance is wholly unacceptable. The chief executive officer has now gone and my office is currently arranging for me to meet the new CEO in the coming days. I will be repeating exactly the same to them: improved performance is absolutely imperative, and if there is any sign that they decide to take their foot off the pedal in relation to resolving the civil service pension scheme and improving the service, I will continue to ensure that there are consequences.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: The remedial report identified that Capita did not have ready what it said it had ready when it took over the scheme. It said that it was going to have the biggest AI-enabled pension scheme ever known, and that clearly was not the case. Its performance has been abysmal, as I have said a number of times in this Chamber. I am not here to make excuses for its performance or for the position that it is now in. In relation to the future of the scheme and bringing it back in-house, it is our manifesto commitment to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and we have not moved away from that at all. My priority at this point is making sure that the service is restored as quickly as possible and that members get the pension they deserve, so I think we need to do everything we can to deliver for scheme members, and then we will look at the future of the pension scheme. As I have said before, we have officials working up different options for its future, as we are with procurement across Government in order to fulfil our manifesto commitment.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I feel for the Minister, because this is a genuinely difficult area, as I think all noble Lords will agree, but this need to keep us all safe, at times by co-operation with the big tech empires, also requires public trust. Will my noble friend, after this leak inquiry has been resolved, consider whether there are any steps that the new Government might take to improve the framework for as much transparency as is possible, at least about the mechanisms that are at play, with a view to improving accountability and trust within the national security framework?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Mark Pritchard
hansard.text: The Minister will know that under the National Security and Investment Act 2021, two Chinese tech companies were called in for review, and then another Chinese tech company was retrospectively called in. Given that the Act contains retrospective powers, is there an ongoing review of tech companies that have contracts with the Government? They may not be Huawei-badged, but they may have links to third countries about which we have concerns. Might a retrospective review under that Act help with some of the issues that the Minister is talking about?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah (Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West) (Lab)
hansard.text: It is a great pleasure to speak in this important debate. Holding it late on a Tuesday night, following a late sitting on a Monday evening, may not be ideal, but given the shifting tectonic plates of AI and the economy, and the level of interest in AI and cyber, the timing of this debate is absolutely critical. I welcome the Bill, as I did on Second Reading and have done throughout its passage. I particularly want to speak to Lords amendment 33, which I see as a necessary attempt to address AI, but I want to share my concerns about the effectiveness of this attempt. No doubt I will do so again when the Minister comes before the Science and Technology Committee. In debates, and in justifying the Bill, the Government have emphasised time and again the social, economic and national security costs of cyber-attacks. I absolutely recognise and support that, and it is incredibly important—in fact, one might argue that the Government are late in addressing the challenges. We are discussing the Bill at a time when AI is putting a booster rocket under the cyber-security challenges coming from criminals, non-state actors and state actors. We have had example after example over the past weeks and months, so it is hugely important that we address this issue. I am glad that the Government are taking the opportunity to address the AI challenge, but Lords amendment 33 does not do so. Lords amendment 33 introduces a new clause, entitled “Functions of the Secretary of State: loss of control of artificial intelligence agent”. It gives the Secretary of State functions in cases where “a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network and information system is or may be attributable to loss of oversight or control of an AI agent”, and in cases where there is a risk of su

hansard.speaker: Miatta Fahnbulleh
hansard.text: We are very clear that there is an economic opportunity from AI, but we need to ensure that we shape it so that it works for the benefit of our communities. That is a combination of focusing on strategic AI projects that have impacts on our wider supply chain and, critically, of ensuring that, where there are data centres, they have a very clear community benefit, whether in what we extract from the companies to invest in communities that host AI centres or wider impacts for the supply chain, chip manufacturing and other things that may come out of this. My hon. Friend is right to raise caution, and I know that communities are worried about AI, but the Government are committed to ensuring that this is AI for good and AI that fundamentally works for our communities.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Alex Sobel (Leeds Central and Headingley) (Lab/Co-op)
hansard.text: The hon. Member is making an excellent speech. She knows that I have tabled my Artificial Superintelligence Bill for discussion on Friday. A regulator is essential in the field of AI. However, I have concerns about Lords amendment 107, because the AI Security Institute, set up at Bletchley, is a research organisation. We are rightly proud of it, as it is the best in the world. It has some of the finest scientists and researchers assessing the most powerful AI. As we know, AI is the fastest moving technology in history. However, we need to ensure the independence of AISI so that it can continue to do its work. We do not want to restrict its research powers in any way. Does the hon. Lady therefore agree that the Government need to bring forward a separate mandatory regulator as part of an AI Bill, rather than rolling those roles together?

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Ian Murray
hansard.text: Quantifying is quite difficult, as is attribution. The JLR situation showed us the costs, but the sophistication of the threats and the wide range of them mean that quantifying them might be quite difficult. The Opposition spokesperson challenged the Government on a number of issues, including the definition of AI and whether the term “automated system” should be used instead. The reason we refer to AI and AI agents is that that is where the harms are happening; the hon. Gentleman talked about basing the provision on the harms, but if he looks at the Hugging Face incident, he will see that the relevant amendments have been made in order to widen the scope in relation to AI, newer technologies and the increasing number of threats.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Ian Murray
hansard.text: That phrasing is in the Bill because the Bill is about extending the measures to cover where we are, in terms of the threats. The mention of AI agents relates to what we are trying to achieve with the Bill. The incidents mentioned by the Chair of the Select Committee—my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West (Dame Chi Onwurah)—and the hon. Member for Exmouth and Exeter East (David Reed) show that the scope needs to be extended. Let me turn to the contribution from the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for Harpenden and Berkhamsted (Victoria Collins). There were a number of questions about small businesses and boards. I think this is the third time in less than seven days that I have said from the Dispatch Box that every single board and every single business in the country needs to reflect on the fact that the risks are real and ensure that it is as cyber-resilient as possible. The NCSC has free tools. On 3 November, we launched a Cyber Essentials funding package for eligible UK small and medium-sized enterprises, which is designed to address the barriers that small organisations face in implementing cyber-security. We understand that this issue has to be on the risk register for all small businesses, and we are trying to put the building blocks in place to ensure that happens. I might have to write to my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West about a practical scenario in relation to Lords amendment 33. How it will work is a matter for consultation, but we will obviously involve the Select Committee in how that comes together. There was a question about putting AISI on a statutory footing. We do not think that that is desirable. My hon. Friend the Member for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel), who is

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill

hansard.text: I thank my right hon. Friend not only for his intervention, but for his expertise and his contribution to the debate on this particularly important issue. In fact, I think that, if anything, it risks muddying the waters. As a responsible Opposition, however, we take at face value the Government's concern that the Secretary of State should have the necessary powers. That being the case, it is essential that the provisions are robust and workable in order to address the risks, not just the latest tools that may be used. Lords amendment 33 focuses specifically on the loss of control of an AI agent. Although that is the relevant technology in use today, the regulation of just this technology presents the risk that the rules become obsolete very quickly in the face of future innovation. The principle is simple: regulate the harm, not the technology. If the Government are correct to say that there is a gap in the reporting requirements on AI agents and loss of control, the harm is the actions and operations of autonomous systems. hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill

hansard.text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Ms Jardine, and I also wish you many happy returns for today. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Rugby (John Slinger) not only for securing this debate, but for his very powerful speech. Members from across the House, but having a team in an office to help them to get things done. When I spoke to new MPs from across the House, the No.1 thing that they were concerned about in those first few weeks of being an MP was not which Select Committee they would be on, when they were going to make their maiden speech or how often they should mention their constituency in the Chamber, but how they were going to get all the casework done. In those first couple of weeks, it felt to me that everybody in Harlow was suddenly becoming homeless at the same t

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Mark Pritchard (The Wrekin) (Con)
hansard.text: What about sovereign capability? The public sector, whether it be the UK intelligence community or other Government Departments, cannot do everything, so the partnership with the private sector is important, particularly for capital-intensive networks. I get that the Government cannot do everything and cannot afford everything, and that partnership with the private sector is absolutely critical, but does the Minister accept that there is still a place for sovereign capability? Regulation cannot cover international private sector companies—US companies, for example, that for political or trade union reasons will not take a particular action that the UK Government want them to.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Graeme Downie (Dunfermline and Dollar) (Lab)
hansard.text: As hon. Members have said this evening, the frontline of hostile state attacks is no longer just in Government networks; it is the fridge in the blood bank, the e-charger on the street and the meter on the wall. I welcome the Bill as the very first step in recognising the real threats that our country faces from cyber-attacks and the need to develop not only defence but resilience. This month, we have seen refrigeration systems hacked in supermarkets across Europe and blood banks in France—I warned about that earlier this year—and we have already seen that EV chargers in the UK are exposed in a similar way. Much of this everyday kit connects to the internet through internet of things small cellular modules, more than 70% of which are manufactured by Chinese firms. Through over-the-air updates, equipment in this country can be changed or switched off from outside it. Hostile states are building leverage over our infrastructure, as we have seen today from Russia and Iran, and we know that China is working towards that in the long term. I therefore welcome Lords amendments 48 to 51, to which the Minister referred, on vendor-related directions, which will give the Secretary of State for the first time the power to stop kit from risky suppliers being installed or used in systems that we all depend on. However, as I have said in the House before, our problem has rarely been a lack of laws; it is often the lack of enforcement. Such powers will be only as good as the will to use them. Energy must be near the front of the queue. We have already seen the EU act on inverters, and the Government rightly turned down the Ming Yang investment in Scotland on security grounds. The equipment on our grid deserves exactly the same scrutiny. Will the Government work with companies in the UK

hansard.text: It is false to claim that cyber security and public safety are mutually exclusive; it is certainly possible to have both, and they are complementary. Companies such as Apple have extraordinary expertise and it is reasonable to expect them to design services that provide strong protection for their users, while retaining a secure means of responding to lawful requirements.

hansard.debate: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill
hansard.speaker: Ian Murray
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to bring this important Bill, which has cross-party support, back to the House. Lords amendment 107 would require the Secretary of State to undertake a comprehensive annual review of the effectiveness of the network and information systems regime. Many issues are raised by this amendment, and I consider the Government to have listened and responded to them carefully. First, the Bill already requires a post-implementation review of the regime. Following concerns raised in the other place, the Government tabled Lords amendment 42 to reduce the timeframe of the review from every five years to every three years. That will allow us to undertake a meaningful and more timely review. Secondly, we have listened to concerns about the sectors in scope of the regime. In the other place, the Minister for Space, Cyber and Regulatory Reform made a clear commitment at the Dispatch Box to assess whether critical sectors not already in scope should be part of the regime and report back to Parliament within 12 months of Royal Assent. I can commit to going further. I confirm that the Government will table an amendment when the Bill goes back to the other place to this effect, so that it is on the face of the Bill. To allow for a flexible approach, it will require the Secretary of State to lay a statement within 12 months of the passage of the Bill, setting out which further activities should be specified as essential under this regime. I can commit that, to inform this statement, the Secretary of State will consider whether activities and services within the UK's critical national infrastructure sectors should be brought within scope of the regime. I can also commit that we will go further and consider advanced manufacturing, electoral infrastructure and political parties

hansard.speaker: Lord Collins of Highbury (Lab)
hansard.text: I understand the point made by my noble friend, but I repeat that there is a clear and robust legislative framework for governing how these issues are addressed. This Parliament and this House have overseen those issues, so we have very clear safeguards. That is the position that we should all support.

hansard.speaker: Lord Collins of Highbury (Lab)

hansard.text: My Lords, while we are disappointed with the tribunal's judgment, we must accept it, because the tribunal does not provide a route for appeal for these types of decisions. hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones
hansard.text: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal's ruling that hearings on the Technical Capability Notice served on Apple must be held in public; and whether they intend to review the use of “neither confirm nor deny” for such notices.

hansard.speaker: Lisa Smart
hansard.text: I think one could do several jobs, but one would not be doing any of them very well. Like others, I have some suggestions of improvements that could be made to the way we do things here, both to encourage Members to do some things and to stop them being able to do others. In my view, Members of the UK Parliament should not be rewarded for posting increasingly divisive content on platforms like X, and yet there is one Member of this House who has earned more than the annual salary of an MP for posting on social media. Every MP in this room and beyond pays the price for that, whichever party we belong to. I do not think every second job is wrong: we should not force NHS doctors, care nurses or legal aid barristers to give up their professional registrations to serve here, and Parliament would be the poorer for losing them. What we do need, though, is proper considered reform of the conduct rules. We should not have MPs marking their own homework. hansard.speaker: David Reed

Lady has a great deal of experience, and I defer to her on many of these matters, but has not the Hugging Face hack identified that some of the autonomous systems we are building will operate and we are going to have to play catch-up to understand what they have actually done?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)

hansard.speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary, Cabinet Office (Sally Jameson)
hansard.text: Before I begin my response, I declare that I have a Capita pension from the Prison Service under the civil service pension scheme. We are aware of the announcement that Capita issued to the market yesterday, including on the appointment of its new chief executive officer, Pablo Andres. The Government routinely monitor the financial health of our strategic suppliers. It would not be appropriate for us to comment on the wider commercial position of Capita as a company, as that is a commercial matter for Capita and its shareholders. Capita's performance on the pension scheme has had unacceptable impacts on people who have dedicated years of their working lives to serving this country, and they deserve better. We are using the most stringent commercial levers, including requiring deliverable plans and withholding payments under the contract that was signed under the last Government. To hold Capita to account, we mandated that it appoint an independent remedial adviser at its own expense. The report identified many weaknesses in Capita's rectification planning, from technology implementation to its overall ambition, which fell well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve. To address that, I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with it to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account. Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita's systems and data to provide us with firmer assurance of the accuracy of the management information and to allow even stronger challenge on Capita's direction and performance. I have put in place dedicated teams to work alongside Capita to agree priorities, improve quality and processes, and ensure that pensions are paid correct

I realise that she is doing an extremely hard job, but will she emphasise in her meeting with the new CEO of Capita that the current system is just not working for my constituents?

hansard.speaker: Dr Neil Shastri-Hurst (Solihull West and Shirley) (Con)
hansard.text: Capita is a reverse Midas: whether on the civil service pension scheme, medicals for armed forces recruitment or a plethora of other contracts across Government, it has repeatedly failed. Will the Minister confirm whether conversations have been had with the senior executives at Capita so that they will not be allowed to fail upwards any longer, and that no further contracts will be even entertained until Capita has sorted out the ones it already has?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I thank the hon. Member for bringing this important issue to the House today and for the questions that he has raised. On what has changed compared with six months ago, following the report of the remedial adviser, Grant Thornton, a new rectification plan was set up in conjunction with the Cabinet Office. Previously, Cabinet Office officials did not even have access to the Capita data and could not see for themselves what the picture was. That is now different, and we have full access to the Capita operation so that we are able to see what is happening with the civil service pension scheme. The rectification plan was built on the back of that, so I think that Members can have more confidence that transparency is there in a way that it was not before, and that we are therefore able to tackle some of the root issues. We still have nearly 150 civil servants from the surge team working with Capita. That has not changed, and it will not change until the pension scheme scenario improves. On the wider issue of contingency, the Government routinely monitor the financial health of all their strategic suppliers, particularly ones as big as Capita, and we work across Government to ensure that relevant contingencies are in place. I am not in a position to discuss that in detail in the Chamber, but that is now routine and lessons were learnt on the back of what happened with Carillion to ensure that the Government do not find themselves in that position again. Capita has up to this point been transparent with the Government and let us know what its position is. While that continues, we will work with it, but it would not be appropriate for me to go into the intricate details of the contingency planning in the Chamber now.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I totally understand the points that the hon. Member raises. I do not want the disruption to get any worse, so whatever we do now has to be about delivering as quickly as possible for scheme members, regardless of what we are working on in parallel in relation to the future of the scheme itself. The Government will seek for Capita to pay back any additional costs we have footed in order to assist it. We have withheld almost £10 million in payments, and Capita is voluntarily receiving 10% less each month in contractual payments. We will use all the levers at our disposal and continue to withhold that money for as long as possible until Capita improves its service and meets the performance indicators that are set out in the contract.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I believe that I should wish the hon. Member a very happy birthday. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear!”] I completely understand the concerns that she raises on behalf of her constituents. I can provide her with the assurance that, as with all strategic suppliers, the Government work across all Departments to ensure that we have good contingency plans in place for any eventuality. That is not just with Capita, but with all strategic suppliers, so Capita is no different. As she will know from my previous statement, we are already looking at contingency because of the state that the pension scheme was in, but the priority is making Capita continue to improve on its service so that we can get money to people as quickly as possible.

hansard.speaker: Christine Jardine (Edinburgh West) (LD)

That is the question they will want to be answered today, and they need reassurance about it. Can the Minister give that?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: The Cabinet Office and the Government have given a huge amount of resources and that will continue to support the scheme and get the service to a good level. I am more satisfied now than I was when I started this job that Capita is putting in sufficient resources. It has stepped up its game. There is a question to be asked about why it did not put more resources in sooner, and that is something I am sure will be discussed long into the future. The priority now is making sure that the resources of both Capita and the Cabinet Office are used to their maximum potential. As it stands, there is sufficient resource, but both Capita and the officials need to crack on to make sure we get those numbers down.

hansard.text: I thank the right hon. Member for raising that important point. In November, Capita was writing to everyone who has a complex case, to detail where their case was in the system. That was a written letter. There is of course a phone line as well. hansard.text: Capita has been open and transparent with the Government, and I was given information beforehand about the problems that it faced. As it stands, the rectification plan is still in place and will continue to run. We have been very clear with Capita that we expect the foot not to be taken off the pedal and that if we are to work to support it, it needs to continue to work on the rectification plan with Cabinet Office officials and the 150-strong surge team that we have put in place. I will continue to monitor that, as will officials, and if there is any change in the level of service, I will obviously address that with Capita and return to the House to set out the next steps. Capita still has significant resources from the Government, including the 150-strong surge team, the officials that are working on this every day and anything else that we can give the company to try to bring the service back up to a decent standard. As it stands, we believe that it has the resources it needs. We will continue to monitor the situation on a daily basis, and if there appears to be any change in its ability to deliver, or in the service that it is delivering, we will of course address that immediately. In relation to the 800 cases and the McCloud remedy, as I said in my recent statement, I will make sure that I update the House on McCloud before the end of the month, and that will happen very shortly. There has been a small improvement on the complex cases. I am happy to write to or meet the Opposition spokesperson to discuss the exact numbers, because I do not have them with me, but we are updating the

hansard.speaker: Victoria Collins (Harpenden and Berkhamsted) (LD)
hansard.text: Steven has dedicated more than 40 years to public service and yet has dwindling savings to get by. Tim, after several errors, has waited more than 18 months for his pension payout from Capita. hansard.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo (Henley and Thame) (LD)

A constituent of mine was told by Capita to sell their car in order to make ends meet. hansard.text: Capita misled my caseworker, and other Members have said that they do not believe a word it says, yet the Minister says that there is the necessary transparency for contingency plans. hansard.text: I thank the right hon. Member for raising that particular issue. Friend wants to write to me with the specific cases that are not being actioned, I will take them up as I have done with other correspondence. Member separately about how his constituents can pursue that. hansard.text: We have currently withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments due to failure, and Capita has taken a voluntary 10% reduction in its monthly payments from Government, so we will continue to monitor that.
