hansard.speaker: Lorraine Beavers (Blackpool North and Fleetwood) (Lab)
hansard.text: Despite improvements that the Cabinet Office have made, my caseworkers and constituents are experiencing a dreadful lack of communication from Capita. Even when some payments are made, there is often no paperwork or explanation. People are being left in the dark; it is a disgrace. What is the Minister doing to ensure that Capita communicates properly with our constituents?

hansard.speaker: Mr Clive Betts (Sheffield South East) (Lab)
hansard.text: I actually feel sorry for the Minister, given her position. She has inherited a terribly difficult situation with Capita, a company that had previously failed to run pension schemes but was handed this scheme last December on a contract let by the previous Government. When the company took over the scheme, it clearly did not have the systems in place to run what is actually a fairly simple job: to administer and pay out pensions. I would just say to the Minister, as I said in the Public Accounts Committee some time ago, that I do not believe a word Capita says any more. If she is in that position as well, does she now recognise that there has to be a fall-back position, and that we have to look seriously at a plan to take this scheme in-house, because I do not think anyone in this Chamber believes that we are going to be in a different position in six months' time if Capita carries on with it?

hansard.speaker: Jim Shannon (Strangford) (DUP)
hansard.text: First, I thank the Minister for her endeavours, which are appreciated by many of us in the House. Many widows and retired civil servants in my constituency of Strangford are in real distress, while waiting months for Capita to process their pensions. Warm words will not pay the heating bills this winter. Will the Minister guarantee that every bereavement and hardship case in that specific 32,600-strong backlog will be cleared before Christmas? Will she set a clear deadline or a target to bring this service back in-house, if Capita fails yet again?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I ask the hon. Member to write to me with that specific case so that I can take it up with Capita.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I agree. It is frankly disgusting that a representative of Capita advised someone to sell their car in order to support themselves financially—it is a complete outrage. I will raise that case with the chief executive and ensure that Capita staff and people dealing with scheme members are properly trained, particularly those dealing with sensitive cases. We continue to work every single day to improve this service, and I will relay all of the hon. Member's points to the chief executive when I meet him.

hansard.speaker: Max Wilkinson (Cheltenham) (LD)
hansard.text: I invite the Minister to share in my frustration and anger at the way GCHQ workers have been treated. These are people who have dedicated their careers to keeping us all safe, and who are now being totally failed by the system that the state they kept safe has set up for them in retirement. Will the Minister look at what is happening with those GCHQ people? As and when the charade of Capita comes to an end, will she also look at setting up a specific scheme so that, in future, GCHQ workers are properly looked after and do not have to put up with Capita, or another company like it, letting them down?

hansard.speaker: Sorcha Eastwood (Lagan Valley) (Alliance)
hansard.text: I have to declare that my husband is a civil servant. Many of my constituents have been impacted by this issue. What I hear—and what I have heard before—is that this is about continuity of service and maintaining a lack of disruption, but constituents are already disrupted. We have presumably paid Capita to carry out this contract. How much money is being spent to remediate this botched Capita contract, and at what point will we cut loose from it and actually deliver for our constituents? Will it be next year, or the year after?

hansard.speaker: Graham Stuart (Beverley and Holderness) (Con)
hansard.text: I will not hold back either. There has been a lot of praise for the Minister today, but every day the situation is getting worse. It is a year ago this month that this Government decided to hand over the contract to Capita, even though the waiting list had grown to 86,000 with MyCSP and the Cabinet Office, in which the Minister sits, knew that Capita did not have the technology in place to take on the contract. This Government made that decision and are responsible, and John from Withernsea is still waiting, seven months on. After 30 years in the Prison Service, he has not received a penny or even a quote, and this Government should apologise. Does the Minister agree?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I am sorry to hear about the experience that the right hon. Member had. I will speak to him afterwards to find out the date of his meeting, so that we can get to the bottom of why the information had not flowed between the two. We definitely want to ensure that the surgeries we are holding are as smooth and efficient as possible, so I am sorry to hear that was not the case. If he writes to me, I am happy to take up the other case he raises. Capita will be delivering on this contract: it has been paid to do a job, so it does not get to just walk away and leave everyone else to clear up the mess. I will continue to push every single day. I will meet the new executive and make absolutely clear my expectations on what Capita will deliver and the progress it will be making, alongside looking at future options.

hansard.speaker: Dr Ellie Chowns (North Herefordshire) (Green)
hansard.text: Significant numbers of my constituents have been badly affected by Capita's failures. I have raised this in the Chamber before, and my caseworkers have done lots of work on this. It is an outsourcing omnishambles, frankly. The Minister has set out the steps she is trying to take to sort this out, but fundamentally it highlights a bigger issue: outsourcing is not working and it does not work. The Minister said the performance of Capita has been “totally, totally unacceptable”. In this context, why are the Government still signing new contracts with Capita, such as the recent UK Health Security Agency contract? She has talked about the Government's commitment to a wave of insourcing, but where is the timetable? Surely it needs to happen now so that we have no more of these failures.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I know my hon. Friend has been diligently campaigning on this issue in recent weeks and months on behalf of many of her constituents who have been affected. On the communication, anyone with a complex case should have had a letter already from Capita this month, or will get one in the next week, as it committed to writing to everyone with a complex case, setting out their situation. When I meet the new chief executive very soon, I will feed back on the need to ensure that paperwork and communications are issued with payments, so that people have the breakdown. We still have the surgeries for Members, which caseworkers and Members can attend to get an update from Capita or the Cabinet Office on the status of a case. I appreciate that people do not always get the answer that they want, but hopefully that will provide reassurance about where the case is in the system.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I thank my hon. Friend for raising the very real hardship that has been faced as a result of Capita's failure. I certainly do not want Emily to tear all her hair out, so we will definitely continue to work at pace to resolve the situation. I have met the Capita executive team regularly since I took up this post, and will meet the new chief executive very shortly. I will continue to relay the day-to-day impact of its performance on people's lives. These are not just numbers; they are people's realities. My hon. Friend highlighted that very well. I assure him, his caseworker and his constituents that I will not let up on ensuring that Capita faces the realities of its failure.

hansard.speaker: Mike Wood (Kingswinford and South Staffordshire) (Con)
hansard.text: Will the Minister tell the House when she was informed of the resignation and what assurances she has received from Capita's incoming chief executive that October's recovery plan will not be derailed? Given Capita's £85 million profit warning and £25 million in extra remediation costs, is the Minister still satisfied that it has the capacity and the resources that it will need to deliver the rectification plan? Last Thursday, I reminded the Minister that she had said five weeks ago that she expected to see visible improvements over the coming weeks. She replied that there had been “small” but insufficient improvements on some “complex cases”. Can she give the House any further update? Specifically, when will the 1,800 complex cases delayed for over a year, including bereavement payments and McCloud remedy cases, finally be cleared? What further contractual penalties or payment withholdings beyond the £10 million already retained will the Government impose? Why have the Government continued to hand Capita further contracts, such as Synergy, when it was already clear that it was failing in its existing commitments to pensioners? Will the Minister now use the powers introduced by the previous Government to consider whether Capita should be debarred from future contracts as a result of its failures? Finally, will the Minister now bring forward contingency plans for use if Capita is unable to fulfil its contract or if it becomes necessary to remove the contract because of its continued failure to deliver required improvements?

hansard.speaker: Richard Tice (Boston and Skegness) (Reform)
hansard.text: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office to make a statement on the UK civil service pension scheme and the performance of Capita plc.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I assure the hon. Member that there will be no warm words exchanged between me and the chief executive when I meet him again. There were not with the last chief executive, either. Warm words are not on the table. I am reluctant to give specific dates or deadlines, particularly because we are focusing on the oldest and most complex cases first. Sometimes they can take days just to resolve. There have been issues around Capita not being clear about what information it wants from members. That can elongate a case. Some of the “business as usual” cases are moving a lot faster, as they do not have the same complexity. As I have said, I expect to see significant progress with Capita in the coming weeks and few short months. The dashboard comes out every fortnight, so people can see for themselves what is happening with the caseloads and where the numbers are going up and down. There is an explanation alongside the dashboard, breaking the numbers down between business as usual and the longer and more complex cases.

hansard.speaker: Sammy Wilson (East Antrim) (DUP)
hansard.text: Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker—I was just about to sit down. May I thank the Minister for the action that she has taken and the access that we have to Cabinet Office officials and to Capita? In fact, only this morning, Helen—a constituent of mine—had her case resolved after nine months. Despite the promises that we have had of significant improvements almost every time this issue has been raised, thousands of people still find themselves in a situation where they cannot get their pension. Although I have no ideological opposition to outsourcing the services of Government, is it not the case that Capita has been so chaotic in this contract, and Government action to change that has been so ineffective, that we really have a case to say, “Bring this in-house”?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: On insourcing, a new unit has been set up and is working with different Departments on insourcing strategies for contracts across Government. That work is ongoing, and I know the Minister for procurement will report back on that when he is ready to update the House. On bringing the Capita contract in-house, I sympathise with the hon. Member's position—as someone who signed up to Labour's 2024 manifesto commitment on insourcing, it is my ideological position as well—but I do not want to do anything that will lead to further or increased disruption for scheme members. We are seeing some improvements—I will not overstate them as it is not for me to defend Capita—on, for example, complex cases coming down, phone line answering and some of the business-as-usual non-complex cases. The improvements are not enough, and I continue to hold Capita's feet to the fire to see further performance improvements, but the scheme members have to be our priority in the coming weeks and months, to get service up to a good standard, and then we can work on what comes next.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: As I have said, the performance of Capita has been totally unacceptable, and it is nothing that any public servant or anyone in this House should expect; we would not accept it among ourselves. I have had a meeting with PCS and all the other unions that represent members who have been affected by this since I came to office, and I am happy to continue having those meetings, to keep people updated on where we are. We committed in our manifesto to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and sitting next to me is the Minister for procurement, my hon. Friend the Member for Gateshead Central and Whickham (Mark Ferguson), who is working on this closely across Government. My priority at the minute, as I said, is ensuring that we get pension scheme members their money as quickly as possible, and I do not want to cause any further disruption to that. I am keen to ensure that this rectification plan works, and that Cabinet Office officials and our 150-person surge team remain working with Capita on the scheme to ensure improvement as soon as possible; and then, of course, we will continue to fulfil our manifesto commitments.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I thank the hon. Member for her contribution. I will continue to work with her and other Opposition spokespeople on the issue. If she wants to write to me about the case she raised, I would be happy to look at it. On the tools at our disposal, we have used all the contractual levers we can, and we will continue to do so. Capita has now been transparent, and has allowed our officials access to all the information that we need. This is a difficult situation for all our scheme members. Before we look at any other options that may cause future disruption, the priority has to be the option that most benefits them, and gives us the best chance of getting the scheme up and running to a good standard for members. I am working on this issue every day, as is the Cabinet Office. Capita is under no illusions about the fact that we expect it to continue to work, day and night, to improve its performance on the contract.

hansard.speaker: Vikki Slade (Mid Dorset and North Poole) (LD)
hansard.text: Laura from Wareham told me that one of the compensations of a lower salary in working time was the promise of a good pension, which she now feels is at risk. She explained that the lump sum due to her in April would have reduced her mortgage payments, which are due to go up in January by £600. Laura has a very simple question: will the compensation from Capita cover those mortgage payments that she never expected to make?

hansard.speaker: Jim Allister (North Antrim) (TUV)
hansard.text: We must never forget that real people, many of them in dire circumstances, are the victims here. I raised one such case when this matter was last before the House—I gave the Minister the details of a constituent who is a stage 4 cancer patient, and who has been waiting since April. I am very disappointed that, despite supplying those details, there has still been no progress in that case. Time is running out for my constituent, but it seems that time never runs out for Capita.

hansard.speaker: Rachel Gilmour (Tiverton and Minehead) (LD)
hansard.text: I have to say that I am running out of pejoratives to describe Capita's performance. Just this morning I learned that Capita has been busily and callously closing unresolved complaints where individuals are still owed money. To my mind, this appears to be nothing more than an attempt to massage its performance figures. Is the Minister aware of that practice, and how can complaints possibly be considered closed when pensioners are still waiting for money that is rightfully theirs?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita's system, so they are able to look at specific cases one by one. That is a relatively new thing that happened only as a consequence of the new rectification plan that was put in place after the remedial adviser went in, and I am confident that we have that level of transparency. However, if the hon. Member wants to raise with me particular instances in which she feels Capita has misled her office, I will take them up with the chief executive when I meet him.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I assure my hon. Friend that I will not hold back when I meet the new Capita chief executive about my expectations, the expectations of the Government and the expectations of the whole House for what we want to see from them in this contract. They will be left under no illusions, just as the last one was not.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: The Cabinet Office and I have been very clear that we expect that, despite the announcement yesterday, there will be no change in Capita and the service that it is expected to deliver in relation to the pension scheme. As my hon. Friend will know from previous statements, the Cabinet Office is looking at all the different options for the future of the pension scheme, and I will report back about that at the appropriate time. I know that he has campaigned really hard on this matter.

hansard.speaker: Euan Stainbank (Falkirk) (Lab)
hansard.text: Alarm bells were ringing last week when Capita told my constituents waiting on delayed payments that interest on those payments would not be automatic and would be taken on a case-by-case basis. Can the Minister reassure us that interest on delayed payments will not be jeopardised by Capita's rapid share price fall over the weekend? What material actions is she taking to build up in-house capacity so that the Government can finally reverse this Tory legacy outsourcing?

hansard.speaker: Dr Kieran Mullan (Bexhill and Battle) (Con)
hansard.text: Karen Allum and Janette Woolgar are just two of several of my constituents who face several months of delays in their payments. For the sake of all of them, what deadline has the Minister given Capita to get this right and have a reasonable service standard? On the question of compensation, with such widespread failure affecting so many people, is it reasonable that they will all have to go through additional hurdles? Can the Minister insist on some kind of standardised and easy-to-access compensation for those experiencing such significant delays?

hansard.speaker: Steve Race (Exeter) (Lab)
hansard.text: I thank the Minister for her support on the Exeter cases that I have raised with her. However, we are still seeing waits of over two months for some of those cases. Some of them are simple admin changes, but more importantly some of the cases are people with life-limiting or very severe illnesses. Will the Minister set out how Capita is prioritising the most vulnerable and time-essential cases that we need to solve?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I am desperately sorry to hear the circumstances of my hon. Friend's constituent. If she writes to me with the details, I will take it up directly. It sounds like a case that should have been resolved before 1 September, so I am more than happy to take that up and ensure Capita deals with it as soon as possible.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: On the insourcing of the scheme and contracts more widely, we have a new insourcing unit that the procurement Minister is leading on. On the scheme itself, we want to ensure we prioritise scheme members and their needs. As I said in my statement, we have already begun to look at different options for the future of the scheme and I will be receiving advice on that in the not-too-distant future, alongside and in parallel to ensuring Capita continues to pull its socks up a lot higher and delivers for scheme members across the country.

hansard.speaker: David Chadwick (Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe) (LD)
hansard.text: My constituents are also facing lengthy and arduous fights to secure their own money from Capita, which we all agree has made a huge mess. Will the Minister commit to ensuring automatic compensation for affected constituents?

hansard.speaker: Amanda Hack (North West Leicestershire) (Lab)
hansard.text: I thank the Minister for her statement and for all her work to try to get this contract back on track. Like so many MPs, my office has a number of bits of casework relating to Capita, and one of the really frustrating things is the capacity we are having to use as MPs to push these cases along for our constituents—constituents like Linda, who has been waiting almost a year for her pension—because of the timeline for complex cases. Could the Minister provide an update on when our constituents should expect to get a resolution and when payments will start to be made to those with complex cases?

hansard.speaker: Mr Jonathan Brash (Hartlepool) (Lab)
hansard.text: My constituent David Ferriday gave 30 years of service to the Crown, and despite retiring roughly six years ago, he says he has still not been able to retire properly because of Capita's abject failure in the administration of his civil service pension. With dozens of case reference numbers, unexplained payments and no meaningful communication, he feels completely failed by this process. Will the Minister intervene directly in cases like David's? Does she agree that this kind of gangster capitalism is exactly why outsourcing always fails the public, and that we should not let Capita anywhere near any future Government contracts?

hansard.speaker: Cat Eccles (Stourbridge) (Lab)
hansard.text: I thank my right hon. Friend for his statement today and for his continued engagement with me and other colleagues. I welcome the commitment to rehumanise the system—something my constituents and I have been crying out for. Last year I tabled an amendment to end outsourcing of assessments to profit-making companies such as Capita and to bring assessors in-house. Does my right hon. Friend agree that we cannot rebuild trust in the system while private contractors remain at its heart, and will he explore whether we can end those contracts much sooner?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: It is absolutely right that no scheme member should be footing the cost for Capita's failure, and if the hon. Member wants to write to me about that case, I will be happy to talk to Capita about it. Some funds have been available to support members, including the Government putting up transitional interest-free loans. However, as I said in a previous answer, I will take up the wider issue of compensation once we have the scheme up and running. I am happy to report back on that, because I accept that a lot of people have suffered as a result of Capita's failure.

hansard.speaker: Caroline Voaden (South Devon) (LD)
hansard.text: I think it is safe to say that the Capita situation is an absolute catastrophe. Mark has given nearly 30 years to the civil service and cannot get a single annual benefit statement, while Julie received a quote in June that differed significantly from the one she was given when she left. She queried it, chased it and was promised a new quote, but it has never arrived. Six months on, she is paying all her bills from her savings, and interest on late payments does not cover that. Will the Minister commit that everyone affected by this scandal will be fully protected from financial loss?

hansard.speaker: Josh Fenton-Glynn (Calder Valley) (Lab)
hansard.text: Things are so bad that I find myself agreeing with the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice). One of my constituents has been waiting since she lost her husband. She contacted me in January, and we still have not heard back. A third of the cases that have come to my office have been solved, but two thirds have not. This contract is not working, so will the Minister look at what options we have to ensure that Capita is not on the table for future procurements like this?

hansard.speaker: Lloyd Hatton (South Dorset) (Lab)
hansard.text: First it was the £90 million contract with the Ministry of Justice, which failed to deliver interpretation services in our courts. Then it was the £1.3 billion contract with the Ministry of Defence, which failed every year to meet recruitment targets in the Army. Now it is the civil service pension scheme fiasco, costing the Cabinet Office some £239 million. Wherever we look, the previous Government signed up to public contracts that effectively fleece the taxpayer, so my question is very simple: what will the Minister do to ensure that this track record of failure, which sits specifically with Capita, is ended once and for all?

hansard.speaker: Liz Saville Roberts (Dwyfor Meirionnydd) (PC)
hansard.text: I thank the Minister for her thorough answers and evident dedication. Jill Hughes MBE of Nefyn received a civil service pension until her death last December. Some 11 months later, her widowed husband David has yet to receive the dependant's pension, even though Capita admits the case is not complex. Mr Hughes is now in a care home and he is at a financial loss directly because of Capita's inaction. It appears to be civil service pension and UK Government policy not to pay interest on delayed payments to bereaved dependants for a number of months. Does she agree, therefore, that this looks very much like an incentive for a profiteering organisation to delay payments, even in non-complex cases?

hansard.speaker: Gavin Robinson (Belfast East) (DUP)
hansard.text: I believe that the Minister deserves credit for the attention she is giving to this issue. I was grateful whenever she made Cabinet Office officials available to deal with individual cases, but I was appalled when I met those officials: they had had no access to the correspondence that we had shared, and they had no knowledge that my constituent had sought a forecast in January, retired in April and had not received a penny for six months. I was grateful that that case was resolved, but it should not have taken the conflict of that call and my disappointment to see progress. I have another constituent who is in the same position, but has been waiting one year for any payment at all. Does the Minister believe that Capita will still be in a position to resolve this issue and the many tens of thousands of others across the United Kingdom, or should it just go?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I am sorry to hear of the experience of my hon. Friend's constituent. I am more than happy to look at that case personally if he writes to me, and I will make sure it is actioned. He highlights Capita's generally abysmal performance and, as I say, I will make no excuses for Capita in this House or any other forum. It has shown that when competition is insufficient and contracts are signed that potentially should not have been or the relevant checks are not done, as was the case under the last Government, we find ourselves in this position. But this Government are committed to making sure that this scheme gets into a far better position for scheme members, and we are, of course, committed to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation.

hansard.speaker: Jonathan Davies (Mid Derbyshire) (Lab)
hansard.text: The Minister was right when she described Capita's administration of the civil service pension scheme as unacceptable, and I want to offer her a few Mid Derbyshire-centred insights from my burgeoning bag of casework on the issue. Gary was due to retire following a brain injury. He was a civil servant at the Department for Work and Pensions, and had asked for his pension calculation three months before he retired; it has not been forthcoming, and the case has been going on for more than a year. Helen's partner, who died, was also a civil servant. The pension arrangements were supposed to support Helen with some money, but she is living off her savings. Both cases have been going on for over a year, and my caseworker Emily is tearing her hair out. Will the Minister make the case to Capita that the human reality of its failure to deal with these issues is that it is causing misery all over the country?

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I thank my right hon. Friend for his engagement with me on this matter. As I have said previously, all Government Departments routinely do contingency planning in relation to strategic suppliers, and this case is no different. I want to ensure that what we do now is in the best interests of scheme members, and we are working with Capita to ensure that the situation for scheme members improves as quickly as possible. He knows my views. He knows that I am committed to the Labour party 2024 manifesto, and so to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation; I have not moved away from that, and neither have the Government. However, in this initial period, we need to ensure that scheme members are the priority, and that services resume for them as quickly as possible.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I concur with my hon. Friend: the service from Capita has been appalling. I will not make any excuses for that today, or on any day. There is an improvement in non-complex, business-as-usual cases being seen in under 30 days, but there is still a big backlog of complex cases, giving us a mixed picture. I said to the House recently that I expect to see significant improvements by the end of this month and before Christmas. We will continue to monitor that, and will return to the House with an update if Capita's performance does not appear to be moving in the right direction.

hansard.speaker: Richard Tice
hansard.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting this urgent question on such a critical matter. The Minister speaks well about the supposed progress, but we have been here before. On 22 April, we discussed this matter and the then Minister, the right hon. Member for Torfaen (Nick Thomas-Symonds), said all the same warm words. The sad truth is that for the 1.7 million members of the pension scheme, the situation is getting worse, not better. When Capita took over the contract, there were about 86,000 outstanding cases; there are now almost 160,000. It is worse than at the beginning of October. I have constituents who are suffering. The number of MPs in the Chamber today indicates that many have constituents who are suffering. We will hear from them, I am sure. It is not good enough, and I warned of the problems. I warned in April that the company faced a financial crisis and that the Government needed a plan B. I said then that the market value of the company was £350 million. It had debts of £500 million. Yesterday, the share price collapsed by 70%. The market value is now £75 million. The chief executive has resigned. The company talks about a rights issue of £190 million. It will be lucky. That is the reality. This company is a critical supplier to the Government. It has over 80 contracts—some £7 billion-worth—running over many, many years. They include the Ministry of Defence's Army recruitment, Royal Navy training, the Department for Work and Pensions and NHS England. This company is too big to fail. We cannot face an equivalent of Carillion plc, but that is where this is going, and I worry. It is all very well saying that we must rely on the commercial company and the shareholders, but there is no guarantee that the shareholders will pony up. This company could well go bust in

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I am sorry to say that I do not agree. The right hon. Gentleman should look at his own party and the last Government, which signed off the levers that this Government have available. The decision taken to hand the contract over at the time was— [ Interruption. ] It was the best option on the table at the time, because of yet another poor contract that was signed by the last Government. I accept that this is a terrible situation for all scheme members. I was a prison officer, and many of my own former colleagues get in touch with me about this issue, and it absolutely needs to be resolved. However, trying to throw the blame for this issue at the current Government and not acknowledging the role of the last Government or, frankly, just focusing on getting this situation better totally misses the point. The Cabinet Office and officials are working day in, day out to improve the situation. This Government are taking steps to ensure that this issue never happens again by looking at insourcing options for the future not just for Capita, but across Government.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I thank the hon. Member for his engagement with me and the Department on this matter. He rightly highlights some of the truly tragic cases that have come to light as a result of Capita's failure. I have said before in this House that it should be absolutely ashamed of its performance. We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point. My position on that has not changed. On contingency planning and what further steps we can take, I have to be careful about what I say in the Chamber, as the hon. Member understands. It is important that we stabilise the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, I assure him that the Government are working across Departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that.

hansard.speaker: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown (North Cotswolds) (Con)
hansard.text: May I thank the Minister for briefing my Committee properly, and the Government for changing the tax rules on lump-sum payments within a week of my raising it in the debate on the Budget? That will provide some reassurance to pensioners in the scheme. We are about to approach the 12-month anniversary of the scheme going live. Sadly, there have been some tragic and dreadful cases in that time. I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme. If the rectification plan does not work, what further steps can the Minister take? For understandable reasons, she does not want to discuss that in the Chamber this afternoon, but if the worst happens and, for some reason or another, Capita cannot carry out the remainder of this contract, she must have a proper contingency plan in place.

hansard.speaker: John McDonnell (Hayes and Harlington) (Lab)
hansard.text: I declare an interest as the chair of the Public and Commercial Services Union parliamentary group. After this long period of failure by Capita, it is time not only to reject the ludicrous suggestion that we give the contract to another outsourcing company, but to take up the civil service union plan of bringing the administration back in house as fast as possible. The problem with also making the competitiveness and growth objective primary—besides the fact that if we add more and more “primary” objectives, the word loses a lot of its meaning—is that the objectives are not always complementary and can be in conflict, as we saw to everybody's detriment in the 2008 global financial crisis. The 2008 crisis had a profound impact on the UK economy, leading to a prolonged period of low growth, rising unemployment and fiscal austerity. When the Institute for Fiscal Studies did an assessment 10 years on, it found there had been a significant cost to our economic growth. The economy was 16%—or £300 billion—smaller than it would have been had it followed the pre-crisis trend, and GDP per capita was nearly £6,000 per person lower than it might have been had pre-crisis trends continued. If we fail to focus properly on the primacy of safety and soundness, policyholder protection and broader financial stability, we know where that ends: it is not good for the economy, and certainly not for taxpayers. I support the secondary competitiveness and growth objective, and I back proportionate decision making in regulators' day-to-day decisions. A councillor can fix a pothole, a charity can run a campaign and a journalist can expose a scandal, but only Parliament can pass, amend and repeal an Act of Parliament. If we do not scrutinise legislation properly, nobody else will do it for us. Yet I suspect every Member has felt the pull of everything else in our job. The Elections Act provided for a substantial programme of evaluation of voter ID requirements, covering the first stand-alone local elections and the first two UK parliamentary general elections following the Act's introduction. hansard.speaker: The Economic Secretary to the Treasury (Lucy Rigby)
hansard.text: It is a real pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Mr Western. I will explain why clause 1 should stand part of the Bill. I will also cover schedule 1, the Government amendments and new clause 3, tabled by the hon. Member for Carshalton and Wallington. The Consumer Credit Act 1974 is more than 50 years old—even older than me. It was designed for a very different credit market, before the creation of the Financial Conduct Authority and long before consumers routinely accessed credit digitally and online. The current framework is complex and, in places, overly prescriptive. Its detailed information requirements can result in lengthy and technical communications that consumers struggle to understand or use. For example, in some circumstances, arrears notices must continue to be sent after a consumer has agreed a repayment plan, potentially causing unnecessary confusion and distress. Clause 1 introduces schedule 1, which provides for detailed reforms to the Consumer Credit Act. Part 1 of the schedule amends the Act, while part 2 makes the necessary minor and consequential amendments to other legislation. The schedule will enable appropriate conduct requirements to be replaced, where necessary, by more flexible FCA rules. I want to be very clear that this is about delivering consumer protections in a clearer, more effective and more adaptable way. Consumers should receive information that is understandable, useful and provided at the right time, helping them to make informed financial decisions. The reforms will create a more agile regulatory regime that is better able to respond as credit products, technology and consumer behaviour evolve, while reducing unnecessary constraints on firms seeking to innovate. Professional bodies will no longer supervise those firms for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing purposes. However, they will continue to regulate their members more widely. It is therefore important that the FCA and the professional bodies co-operate and share relevant information to ensure that the regime functions effectively and any burdens on firms are minimised. It enables regulations to be made to provide for co-operation and information sharing powers between the FCA and the professional bodies responsible for the wider regulation and supervision of professional services providers. I also welcomed the confirmation that discussions are taking place with the Home Office on this matter. However, having the power to request information is not the same as having the clear, consistent and legally prescribed mechanism that we ought to expect when considering new legislation that should be designed to safeguard the integrity of the process. I do not believe that it is good enough for the Government to say simply that the details of data sources would be set out in secondary legislation and later guidance. That is far more positive, at least in spirit, than a rather more regressive contemporary trend, which is to put caveats on certain types of people voting. I draw the Committee's attention to a shocking report that came out this week, What Britain's New Establishment Thinks A nd Why I t Matters , in which 1,000 higher professionals were polled. It reminded me, though, of those grim days post 2016, when a particular type of remainer—a sore loser, to say the least—started to complain that leave voters were uneducated, stupid or ignorant and did not have enough qualifications to be trusted ever again. hansard.text: The Procurement Act 2023 provides Government with the statutory power to launch a formal investigation that can lead to debarment, either for severe breaches of contract or for poor performance. That is different from what happened before; it allow us to take into account poor performance, and not just technical ways that a company has failed. I am not in a position to confirm or deny whether a supplier is under active consideration for, or subject to, a debarment investigation, but I reiterate that it is an option that Government now have when there is poor performance by any strategic supplier.

hansard.speaker: Sally Jameson
hansard.text: I am sorry to hear about the experience that the hon. Member's constituent had. I am glad that they now have their money, but I recognise that lots of people are still waiting to be paid. Nine months is totally unacceptable, and I will not make excuses for that. Turning to the future arrangements for the pension scheme and contracts more widely, the Procurement Act 2023 allows the Government to look at poor performance when issuing new contracts, and we will continue to do that.
